claims.text: Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi enhances local solute fluctuations in the resulting FeNiCrMn alloy.
The enhanced solute fluctuations primarily involve Cr and Mn.
Local Cr–Mn solute fluctuations modify local stacking-fault energies.
Local solute fluctuations or chemical short-range order increase dislocation-obstacle strength and locally pin dislocations.
Solute-induced pinning is especially effective in Co-free FeNiCrMn at low temperatures and high strain rates.
Solute-induced dislocation pinning produces serrated plastic flow.
Solute-induced dislocation pinning increases strain hardening in the low-temperature, high-strain-rate regime.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation allows dislocations to overcome the transient solute barriers.
Lower strain rates allow dislocations to overcome the transient solute barriers.
Overcoming the transient barriers causes a transition from serrated to smooth, continuous plastic flow.
At low temperatures, Co-free FeNiCrMn has higher yield strength than identically processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi because of stronger solute pinning.
At low temperatures, Co-free FeNiCrMn has greater strain-rate sensitivity than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Co-free FeNiCrMn exhibits more pronounced stress–strain serrations than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at low temperature and high strain rate.
Co-free FeNiCrMn exhibits higher strain hardening than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at low temperature and high strain rate.
The Co-free alloy undergoes a distinct temperature- or strain-rate-dependent transition from pinned serrated flow to smooth flow.
Dislocation-based plasticity dominates Co-free FeNiCrMn between approximately 77 K and 600–700 K and between strain rates of 10^-4 and 10^-1 s^-1.
Phonon drag may become significant at strain rates above the stated range.
Dynamic recrystallization may become significant at high homologous temperatures outside the stated range.
The proposed starting Co-free FeNiCrMn material is a single-phase solid solution produced from the melt.
The Co-free and Co-containing alloys can be prepared with identical starting microstructures for the controlled comparison.
